subject: math
title: Geometry I: Perimeter, Area, Circles, Composite Figures, and the Pythagorean Theorem
objectives: Students will find the perimeter of rectangles, squares, and other polygons and distinguish perimeter from area in real-world problems.
Students will find the area of rectangles, squares, triangles, parallelograms, and trapezoids, knowing which formulas are on the GED formula sheet and which must be memorized.
Students will find the circumference and area of a circle from its radius or diameter, using 3.14 or the π key as directed.
Students will find the area and perimeter of composite figures by adding or subtracting simple shapes.
Students will use the Pythagorean theorem to find a missing side of a right triangle and to decide whether a triangle is a right triangle.
teach:
Objectives

  • Find the perimeter of polygons and explain the difference between perimeter (distance around) and area (space inside).
  • Find the area of rectangles, squares, triangles, parallelograms, and trapezoids, knowing which formulas appear on the GED formula sheet and which must be memorized.
  • Find the circumference and area of a circle from its radius or diameter, using 3.14 or the π key.
  • Find the area and perimeter of composite figures by splitting them into simple shapes or subtracting a missing piece.
  • Use the Pythagorean theorem to find a missing side of a right triangle and to decide whether a triangle is a right triangle.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen; grid paper (or a grid on screen) for drawing rectangles and triangles
  • Printed or digital copies of this week's Student Lesson and Study Sheet
  • A copy of the GED formula sheet (or the formulas written on the board exactly as they appear: parallelogram A = bh, trapezoid A = ½h(b1 + b2), and the Pythagorean theorem a2 + b2 = c2)
  • A scientific calculator with a π key and a square root key
  • Optional: a paper rectangle and scissors to show that a parallelogram can be cut and rearranged into a rectangle; a string and a round lid to measure circumference

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5Five quick calculations that review multiplying, halving, squaring, and square roots.
Direct instruction20Perimeter and rectangle area (4 min), triangles, parallelograms, and trapezoids (5 min), circles (4 min), composite figures (3 min), Pythagorean theorem (4 min). Model the worked examples.
Guided practice15Students work five problems with you or in pairs. Insist on a labeled sketch for every problem.
Independent practice15Students start the 12 weekly practice items (items 1–8 in class; finish at home).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding, which formulas to memorize, and this week's study plan.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Post these as students arrive. A calculator is allowed for number 5 only.

  1. 8 × 7
  2. ½ × 10 × 6
  3. 52
  4. √81
  5. 3.14 × 4

Answers: (1) 56   (2) 30   (3) 25   (4) 9   (5) 12.56

Tell students every one of these calculations appears in today's lesson: multiplying (rectangles), taking half (triangles), squaring and square roots (circles and the Pythagorean theorem), and multiplying by 3.14 (circles).

Direct Instruction (20 minutes)

1. Perimeter and the area of rectangles (about 4 minutes)

Talking points:

  • Perimeter is the distance around a figure. Add the lengths of all the sides. The answer is a length, so the units are plain units: feet, meters, inches.
  • For a rectangle, P = 2l + 2w. For a square, P = 4s. Students do not need a formula for other polygons: just add every side.
  • Area is the amount of surface inside a figure, measured in square units (square feet, ft2). Draw a 4-by-3 rectangle on grid paper and count the 12 squares, then show 4 × 3 = 12.
  • Rectangle: A = lw. Square: A = s2. These are not on the GED formula sheet. Students must know them.
  • Real-life cue words: fence, trim, border, baseboard, frame, and “around” signal perimeter. Carpet, paint, tile, sod, and “cover” signal area.

Worked Example 1 (perimeter and area). A bedroom is 15 feet long and 11 feet wide. How many feet of baseboard are needed to go around the room (ignore the door)? How many square feet of flooring cover the floor?

Baseboard goes around the edge, so find the perimeter:

P = 2(15) + 2(11) = 30 + 22 = 52 feet

Flooring covers the surface, so find the area:

A = 15 × 11 = 165 square feet

Answer: 52 feet of baseboard; 165 square feet of flooring. Point out that the same room gives two very different numbers depending on the question asked.

2. Triangles, parallelograms, and trapezoids (about 5 minutes)

Talking points:

  • A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides. A = bh, where h is the height: the perpendicular (straight up-and-down) distance between the bases, not the slanted side. If you have the paper model, cut a triangle off one end and slide it to the other end: the parallelogram becomes a rectangle with the same base and height. This formula is on the formula sheet.
  • A triangle is half of a parallelogram. A = ½bh. Draw a diagonal across a rectangle to show two equal triangles. This formula is not on the formula sheet.
  • A trapezoid has exactly one pair of parallel sides, called the bases b1 and b2. A = ½h(b1 + b2). In words: average the two bases, then multiply by the height. This formula is on the formula sheet.
  • Height is always measured at a right angle to the base. On a diagram, look for the small square corner symbol or a dashed line.

Worked Example 2 (triangle and trapezoid). (a) A triangular sail has a base of 8 feet and a height of 12 feet. Find its area. (b) A garden bed is shaped like a trapezoid with parallel sides of 9 meters and 15 meters. The distance between the parallel sides is 6 meters. Find its area.

(a) A = ½bh = ½ × 8 × 12 = ½ × 96 = 48 square feet

(b) A = ½h(b1 + b2) = ½ × 6 × (9 + 15)

9 + 15 = 24, so A = ½ × 6 × 24 = 3 × 24 = 72 square meters

Answer: (a) 48 ft2; (b) 72 m2. Ask what someone gets if they forget the ½ in part (a): 96, a very common wrong answer choice.

3. Circles (about 4 minutes)

Talking points:

  • The radius r goes from the center to the edge. The diameter d goes all the way across through the center. d = 2r and r = d ÷ 2.
  • Circumference is the perimeter of a circle: C = πd or C = 2πr.
  • Area: A = πr2. Square the radius first, then multiply by π. If you are given the diameter, cut it in half before you square.
  • Neither circle formula is on the GED formula sheet. Have students say them out loud: “C equals pi d; A equals pi r squared.”
  • π is about 3.14. A GED question will tell students either to use 3.14 or to use the π key on the calculator, and how to round. Follow those directions exactly, because the answer choices are built from them.

Worked Example 3 (circumference and area). A circular patio has a diameter of 14 feet. Using 3.14 for π, find (a) the distance around the patio and (b) the area of the patio.

(a) C = πd = 3.14 × 14 = 43.96 feet

(b) The radius is 14 ÷ 2 = 7 feet.

r2 = 7 × 7 = 49

A = 3.14 × 49 = 153.86 square feet

Answer: 43.96 feet around; 153.86 ft2. Show the trap: using 14 in the area formula gives 3.14 × 196 = 615.44, four times too large.

4. Composite figures (about 3 minutes)

Talking points:

  • A composite figure is made of simple shapes. Two strategies: add the pieces, or take a big shape and subtract the missing piece.
  • Find any missing side lengths first by using the sides you know (opposite sides of a rectangle are equal).
  • For perimeter, trace only the outside edge. Lines you draw to split the figure are not part of the perimeter.

Worked Example 4 (composite figure). A rug is a rectangle 10 meters long and 6 meters wide with a half-circle attached to one of its 6-meter ends, so the 6-meter end is the diameter of the half-circle. Use the π key and round to the nearest tenth. Find the area and the perimeter of the rug.

Area. Rectangle: 10 × 6 = 60 m2

Half-circle: radius = 6 ÷ 2 = 3, so ½ × π × 32 = 4.5π ≈ 14.137 m2

Total: 60 + 14.137 = 74.137 ≈ 74.1 m2

Perimeter. The outside edge is two 10-meter sides, one 6-meter end, and the curved half of a circle. (The other 6-meter end is inside the rug, so it does not count.)

Straight sides: 10 + 10 + 6 = 26 m

Curved edge: ½ × π × 6 = 3π ≈ 9.425 m

Total: 26 + 9.425 = 35.425 ≈ 35.4 m

Answer: area ≈ 74.1 m2; perimeter ≈ 35.4 m.

5. The Pythagorean theorem (about 4 minutes)

Talking points:

  • It works only for right triangles (one 90° angle). The two sides that form the right angle are the legs (a and b). The longest side, across from the right angle, is the hypotenuse (c).
  • a2 + b2 = c2. This is on the formula sheet, but the sheet does not tell students which side is c. That is the skill to practice.
  • Finding the hypotenuse: square the legs, add, take the square root. Finding a leg: square the hypotenuse and the known leg, subtract, take the square root.
  • Sanity check: the hypotenuse is always the longest side, but shorter than the two legs added together.
  • Common whole-number sets (Pythagorean triples) to recognize: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, and multiples such as 6-8-10.

Worked Example 5 (Pythagorean theorem). (a) A television screen is 32 inches wide and 24 inches tall. Screens are sold by the length of the diagonal. What is the diagonal? (b) A 17-foot ladder leans against a wall with its base 8 feet from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?

(a) The diagonal is the hypotenuse. 322 + 242 = c2

1,024 + 576 = 1,600, and √1,600 = 40 inches

(b) The ladder is the hypotenuse (17). The distance from the wall (8) is a leg. Find the other leg:

82 + b2 = 172, so 64 + b2 = 289

b2 = 289 − 64 = 225, and √225 = 15 feet

Answer: (a) 40 inches; (b) 15 feet. Ask what happens if a student adds in part (b): √(289 + 64) = √353 ≈ 18.8 feet, which is longer than the ladder itself. That is impossible, so the student knows to subtract.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Have students sketch and label each figure before computing. Work the first one together; let pairs try the rest, then review.

  1. A square tile has sides of 9 cm. Find its perimeter and area.
  2. A parallelogram has a base of 14 inches, a slanted side of 8 inches, and a height of 6 inches. Find its area and perimeter.
  3. A circular fountain has a radius of 5 meters. Using 3.14 for π, find its circumference and area.
  4. A right triangle has legs of 7 and 24. Find the hypotenuse.
  5. A wall is 12 feet wide and 8 feet tall. It has a door 3 feet wide and 7 feet tall. How many square feet of wall need paint?

Answers:

(1) P = 4 × 9 = 36 cm; A = 9 × 9 = 81 cm2

(2) A = bh = 14 × 6 = 84 in2 (not 14 × 8 = 112). P = 2(14) + 2(8) = 28 + 16 = 44 in. The perimeter uses the slanted side; the area uses the height.

(3) C = 2 × 3.14 × 5 = 31.4 m; A = 3.14 × 52 = 3.14 × 25 = 78.5 m2

(4) 72 + 242 = 49 + 576 = 625; √625 = 25

(5) Wall: 12 × 8 = 96 ft2. Door: 3 × 7 = 21 ft2. Paint: 96 − 21 = 75 ft2

Checks for Understanding

  • Ask: “You are buying a fence for a yard. Do you need perimeter or area? What about grass seed?” Expected: fence is perimeter (feet); seed is area (square feet).
  • Ask: “A circle has a diameter of 18. What number goes into the area formula?” Expected: the radius, 9.
  • Ask: “Which three area formulas are not on the formula sheet?” Expected: rectangle (A = lw), triangle (A = ½bh), and circle (A = πr2); circumference (C = πd) is also not on the sheet.
  • Ask: “Is a triangle with sides 10, 24, and 26 a right triangle?” Expected: yes, because 102 + 242 = 100 + 576 = 676 = 262.
  • Ask: “In the Pythagorean theorem, when do you subtract?” Expected: when the hypotenuse is known and you are finding a leg.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Forgetting the ½ in the triangle formula. Students multiply base × height and stop. Correction: remind them that a triangle is half of a rectangle. Have them sketch the rectangle around the triangle.

Using the slanted side as the height. In parallelograms, triangles, and trapezoids, students grab the side length they see. Correction: the height must meet the base at a right angle. Look for the square corner mark or dashed line.

Mixing up radius and diameter. Using the diameter in A = πr2 makes the area four times too big. Correction: circle the word “radius” or “diameter” in the problem and write r = ___ before anything else.

Adding when you should subtract in the Pythagorean theorem. Correction: label c first. If c is the unknown, add; if c is given, subtract. Then check that the hypotenuse is the longest side.

Counting inside lines in a composite perimeter, or overlapping pieces in a composite area. Correction: trace the outside edge with a finger before adding; shade each piece only once.

Wrong units. Perimeter is in feet; area is in square feet. On the GED, a wrong-unit answer choice is often present. Correction: write the unit with every answer.

Differentiation

Support: Use grid paper so students can count squares and confirm A = lw and A = ½bh. Give a formula card with each shape drawn and its height marked. Start Pythagorean problems with the 3-4-5 triangle and let students check by counting on grid paper. Allow 3.14 before introducing the π key.

Stretch: Work backward: a rectangle has an area of 96 ft2 and a length of 12 ft; find the perimeter (width 8, P = 40 ft). A circle has a circumference of 62.8 ft (use 3.14); find its area (r = 10, A = 314 ft2). Find the distance between the points (1, 2) and (7, 10) on a coordinate plane by drawing a right triangle (legs 6 and 8, distance 10).

How This Shows Up on the GED

  • Geometry appears in both parts of the test, so students need the rectangle, triangle, and circle formulas memorized and need to find the parallelogram and trapezoid formulas and the Pythagorean theorem on the formula sheet quickly.
  • Typical wordings: “How many feet of fencing…,” “What is the area, in square feet, of…,” “Use 3.14 for π,” “Round your answer to the nearest tenth,” “How far is the top of the ladder from the ground?”
  • Formats: multiple choice with distractors built from common errors (forgot ½, used diameter for radius, gave perimeter instead of area); fill-in-the-blank numeric answers; drag-and-drop matching figures to areas; drop-down menus completing statements.
  • Diagrams are common, and students are expected to read side lengths and heights from labels. Composite figures (L-shaped rooms, windows with a half-circle top, yards with a shed) are favorites.
  • Remind students that this week's Practice GED covers the whole math test, including this week's geometry.
student:
Welcome to Week 5

This week you will measure flat shapes: how far it is around them and how much space they cover. These skills show up constantly in daily life (fencing a yard, buying carpet, painting a wall) and on the GED math test. Some formulas are on the GED formula sheet, and some are not. This lesson tells you which ones you must memorize.

1. Perimeter: The Distance Around

Perimeter is the total length of all the sides of a figure. To find it, add every side. Perimeter is a length, so it is measured in units such as inches, feet, or meters.

  • Rectangle: P = 2l + 2w (two lengths plus two widths)
  • Square: P = 4s
  • Any other polygon: add all the sides.

Clue words: fence, border, trim, frame, and “around” usually mean perimeter.

2. Area of Rectangles, Squares, and Triangles

Area is the amount of surface inside a figure. It is measured in square units: square inches (in2), square feet (ft2), square meters (m2). Carpet, paint, tile, and “cover” usually mean area.

Memorize these. They are NOT on the GED formula sheet.

  • Rectangle: A = lw (length × width)
  • Square: A = s2
  • Triangle: A = ½bh (half of base × height)

The height of a triangle is the straight up-and-down distance from the base to the opposite corner. It meets the base at a right angle (90°). It is not always one of the sides.

Example 1. A picture frame is 20 inches tall and 16 inches wide. How much trim goes around the frame, and how much glass covers the picture?

Trim goes around, so find the perimeter: P = 2(20) + 2(16) = 40 + 32 = 72 inches

Glass covers the surface, so find the area: A = 20 × 16 = 320 square inches

Answer: 72 inches of trim; 320 in2 of glass

Example 2. A triangular flag has a base of 18 inches and a height of 10 inches. Find its area.

A = ½bh = ½ × 18 × 10

18 × 10 = 180, and half of 180 is 90.

Answer: 90 square inches

3. Parallelograms and Trapezoids

These two formulas are on the GED formula sheet, so you do not have to memorize them. You do need to know what the letters mean.

  • Parallelogram (two pairs of parallel sides): A = bh. Use the height, not the slanted side.
  • Trapezoid (exactly one pair of parallel sides): A = ½h(b1 + b2). The two parallel sides are the bases. Add the bases, multiply by the height, then take half.

Example 3. A section of a deck is shaped like a trapezoid. Its parallel sides are 10 feet and 16 feet long, and the distance between them is 7 feet. How many square feet is this section?

A = ½h(b1 + b2) = ½ × 7 × (10 + 16)

10 + 16 = 26

½ × 7 × 26 = 7 × 13 = 91

Answer: 91 square feet

Watch out: If a parallelogram has a base of 10, a slanted side of 6, and a height of 5, the area is 10 × 5 = 50, not 10 × 6 = 60. The slanted side is used only for the perimeter.

4. Circles

The radius (r) goes from the center of a circle to its edge. The diameter (d) goes all the way across through the center, so d = 2r. The distance around a circle is called the circumference. The number π (pi) is about 3.14.

Memorize these. They are NOT on the GED formula sheet.

  • Circumference: C = πd (or C = 2πr)
  • Area: A = πr2 (square the radius first, then multiply by π)

A GED question will tell you to use 3.14 or the π key on your calculator. Follow its directions about rounding, too.

Example 4. A round pizza has a diameter of 16 inches. Using 3.14 for π, find the length of its crust edge (circumference) and its area.

C = πd = 3.14 × 16 = 50.24 inches

For area you need the radius: r = 16 ÷ 2 = 8 inches

A = πr2 = 3.14 × 82 = 3.14 × 64 = 200.96 square inches

Answer: 50.24 inches around; about 200.96 in2

5. Composite Figures

A composite figure is made of two or more simple shapes. Use one of two strategies:

  1. Add: split the figure into rectangles, triangles, or half-circles, find each area, and add.
  2. Subtract: find the area of a large shape, then subtract the part that is missing.

For the perimeter of a composite figure, add only the lengths along the outside edge.

Example 5. A backyard is a rectangle 30 feet by 20 feet. A shed that is 8 feet by 5 feet sits in the yard. How many square feet of the yard are covered by grass?

Whole yard: 30 × 20 = 600 ft2

Shed: 8 × 5 = 40 ft2

Grass: 600 − 40 = 560 ft2

Answer: 560 square feet

6. The Pythagorean Theorem

A right triangle has one 90° angle. The two sides that make the right angle are the legs, a and b. The longest side, across from the right angle, is the hypotenuse, c. This formula is on the formula sheet:

a2 + b2 = c2

  • Finding the hypotenuse: square both legs, add, then take the square root.
  • Finding a leg: square the hypotenuse and the known leg, subtract, then take the square root.

Example 6. (a) A support wire runs from the top of a 12-foot pole to a point on the ground 5 feet from the bottom of the pole. How long is the wire? (b) A 10-foot ladder leans against a wall with its base 6 feet from the wall. How high does it reach?

(a) The wire is the hypotenuse: 122 + 52 = 144 + 25 = 169, and √169 = 13 feet

(b) The ladder is the hypotenuse: 62 + b2 = 102, so 36 + b2 = 100

b2 = 100 − 36 = 64, and √64 = 8 feet

Answer: (a) 13 feet; (b) 8 feet

Check yourself: the hypotenuse must be the longest side. If your “leg” comes out longer than the hypotenuse, you added when you should have subtracted.

Try It

1. A rectangular parking lot is 23 meters long and 9 meters wide. What is its perimeter?

Show answer

P = 2(23) + 2(9) = 46 + 18 = 64 meters

2. A triangle has a base of 15 inches and a height of 8 inches. What is its area?

Show answer

A = ½ × 15 × 8 = ½ × 120 = 60 square inches

3. A circular rug has a diameter of 20 centimeters. Using 3.14 for π, what is its area?

Show answer

r = 20 ÷ 2 = 10. A = 3.14 × 102 = 3.14 × 100 = 314 square centimeters

4. A trapezoid has bases of 5 feet and 11 feet and a height of 4 feet. What is its area?

Show answer

A = ½ × 4 × (5 + 11) = 2 × 16 = 32 square feet

5. A park is a rectangle 80 meters long and 60 meters wide. How much shorter is it to walk diagonally across the park than to walk along two sides from one corner to the opposite corner?

Show answer

Along two sides: 80 + 60 = 140 m. Diagonal: 802 + 602 = 6,400 + 3,600 = 10,000, and √10,000 = 100 m. The diagonal is 140 − 100 = 40 meters shorter.
post:
Summary of Key Points

  • Perimeter is the distance around a figure (units: feet, meters). Area is the surface inside (units: square feet, square meters).
  • Memorize: rectangle A = lw, square A = s2, triangle A = ½bh, circle C = πd and A = πr2. These are not on the GED formula sheet.
  • On the formula sheet: parallelogram A = bh, trapezoid A = ½h(b1 + b2), and the Pythagorean theorem a2 + b2 = c2.
  • Height is always measured at a right angle to the base, never along a slanted side.
  • Radius is half the diameter. Use the radius in A = πr2.
  • Composite figures: add the pieces or subtract the missing piece. For perimeter, count only the outside edge.
  • Pythagorean theorem: add squares to find the hypotenuse; subtract squares to find a leg. The hypotenuse is always the longest side.

Exit Ticket

1. What is the area of a rectangle that is 12 cm long and 7 cm wide?

Show answer

12 × 7 = 84 cm2

2. What is the area of a triangle with a base of 9 ft and a height of 4 ft?

Show answer

½ × 9 × 4 = ½ × 36 = 18 ft2

3. Using 3.14 for π, what is the circumference of a circle with a radius of 3 inches?

Show answer

C = 2πr = 2 × 3.14 × 3 = 18.84 inches

4. A right triangle has legs of 8 and 15. How long is the hypotenuse?

Show answer

82 + 152 = 64 + 225 = 289; √289 = 17

5. A wall is 10 feet wide and 8 feet tall with a window 3 feet wide and 4 feet tall. How many square feet of wall are there to paint?

Show answer

Wall: 10 × 8 = 80 ft2. Window: 3 × 4 = 12 ft2. Paint: 80 − 12 = 68 ft2

Reflection

  • Which formulas do you already know by heart, and which ones do you need to keep practicing until you can write them from memory?
  • Think of a home or work project (painting, flooring, fencing, gardening). Would it need perimeter, area, or both? What measurements would you take?
  • When you missed a problem this week, was the mistake in choosing the formula, finding the right measurement (radius vs. diameter, height vs. slanted side), or the arithmetic?

Test-Taking Strategy: Sketch, Label, Then Choose the Formula

For every geometry question, draw a quick sketch on your note board even if a diagram is given, and write each measurement where it belongs. Then ask: is this question about the distance around (perimeter), the space inside (area), or a missing side of a right triangle? Write the formula before you put in numbers. Finally, check the units in the answer choices. Many wrong choices are the right number for the wrong question, such as a perimeter when the question asked for area.

  1. Sketch and label every side; find missing sides from opposite sides.
  2. Split into simple shapes and add, or take a big shape and subtract the missing part.
  3. Perimeter: outside edge only.

Top Mistakes

  • Forgetting ½ for triangles
  • Using a slanted side as the height
  • Using the diameter in A = πr2
  • Adding instead of subtracting to find a leg
  • Giving perimeter when area was asked

items.prompt: Dana wants to put a fence around all four sides of a rectangular garden that is 18 feet long and 12 feet wide. How many feet of fencing does she need?
items.hint: Fencing goes around the edge, so add all four sides: two lengths and two widths.
items.explain:
Fencing goes around the garden, so find the perimeter.

P = 2l + 2w = 2(18) + 2(12)

2(18) = 36 and 2(12) = 24

36 + 24 = 60 feet

The choice 30 feet adds only one length and one width (half the perimeter). The choice 216 feet is 18 × 12, the area in square feet, which answers a different question. The choice 72 feet treats the garden as a square with sides of 18.

items.prompt: A triangular piece of fabric has a base of 14 inches and a height of 9 inches. What is the area of the fabric?
items.hint: The area of a triangle is half of base times height: A = ½bh. This formula is not on the formula sheet.
items.explain:
A = ½bh = ½ × 14 × 9

14 × 9 = 126

½ × 126 = 63 square inches

The choice 126 forgets to take half. The choice 23 adds 14 + 9 instead of multiplying. The choice 31.5 takes half twice.

items.prompt: A circular rug has a diameter of 10 feet. Binding tape will be sewn around the entire edge of the rug. Using 3.14 for π, how many feet of binding tape are needed?
items.hint: The distance around a circle is the circumference: C = πd. You are given the diameter.
items.explain:
The edge of a circle is its circumference. You know the diameter, so use C = πd.

C = 3.14 × 10 = 31.4 feet

A common mistake is to use the area formula: 3.14 × 52 = 78.5, which is the number of square feet the rug covers, not the length of its edge. Another mistake is to double the diameter: 2 × 3.14 × 10 = 62.8. The formula 2πr uses the radius (5), not the diameter.

items.prompt: A circular clock face has a radius of 6 inches. What is the area of the clock face? Use the π key on your calculator and round to the nearest tenth of a square inch.
items.hint: A = πr<sup>2</sup>. Square the radius first, then multiply by π.
items.explain:
A = πr2 = π × 62

62 = 36

π × 36 ≈ 113.097

Rounded to the nearest tenth: 113.1 square inches

The choice 37.7 is the circumference (2 × π × 6 ≈ 37.699). The choice 452.4 uses the diameter, 12, in place of the radius (π × 144 ≈ 452.389). The choice 18.8 multiplies π by 6 without squaring.

items.prompt:
The figure shows a parallelogram. Its base is 12 centimeters, its slanted side is 7 centimeters, and its height (the dashed line) is 5 centimeters.

What is the area of the parallelogram?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 180' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='40,140 220,140 270,60 90,60' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='90' y1='60' x2='90' y2='140' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><polyline points='90,130 100,130 100,140' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='130' y='162' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>12 cm</text><text x='58' y='100' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>7 cm</text><text x='97' y='108' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>5 cm</text></svg>
figure.alt: A parallelogram with a bottom base labeled 12 cm, a slanted left side labeled 7 cm, and a dashed vertical height labeled 5 cm drawn from the top-left corner down to the base, meeting it at a right angle.

items.hint: The formula sheet gives A = bh for a parallelogram. The height meets the base at a right angle; it is not the slanted side.
items.explain:
A = bh, where h is the perpendicular height.

A = 12 × 5 = 60 square centimeters

The choice 84 uses the slanted side as the height (12 × 7). The choice 30 takes half, which is the triangle formula. The choice 38 is the perimeter: 2(12) + 2(7) = 24 + 14 = 38 centimeters.

items.prompt: Find the area of each figure. Then drag each figure into the bin that shows its area. All measurements are in units, and heights are perpendicular to the bases.
items.hint: Rectangle: lw. Triangle: ½bh. Parallelogram: bh. Trapezoid: ½h(b<sub>1</sub> + b<sub>2</sub>).
items.explain:
Rectangle: 8 × 5 = 40 → 40 square units

Triangle (base 10, height 4): ½ × 10 × 4 = 20 → 20 square units

Parallelogram: 10 × 4 = 40 → 40 square units

Trapezoid (bases 3 and 7, height 4): ½ × 4 × (3 + 7) = 2 × 10 = 20 → 20 square units

Triangle (base 16, height 10): ½ × 16 × 10 = 80 → 80 square units

Trapezoid (bases 12 and 8, height 8): ½ × 8 × (12 + 8) = 4 × 20 = 80 → 80 square units

Notice that a triangle and a parallelogram with the same base and height do not have the same area: the triangle is half. Forgetting the ½ would put the first triangle in the 40 bin.

items.prompt: A 13-foot ladder leans against the side of a house. The bottom of the ladder is 5 feet from the base of the wall, and the ground is level. How high up the wall does the top of the ladder reach?
items.hint: The wall, the ground, and the ladder form a right triangle. The ladder is the hypotenuse, so subtract the squares.
items.explain:
The ladder is the hypotenuse (c = 13), and the distance from the wall is a leg (a = 5). Find the other leg, b.

a2 + b2 = c2, so 52 + b2 = 132

25 + b2 = 169

b2 = 169 − 25 = 144

b = √144 = 12 feet

The choice 13.9 comes from adding the squares (√(169 + 25) = √194 ≈ 13.9); that would make the wall height longer than the ladder, which is impossible. The choices 8 and 18 subtract or add the side lengths without squaring.

items.prompt:
A right triangle has legs that are 9 units and 12 units long.

Choose the option that makes each statement true.

The hypotenuse of the triangle is {{0}} units long.

The perimeter of the triangle is {{1}} units.
items.hint: Use a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup> = c<sup>2</sup> to find the hypotenuse first. The perimeter adds all three sides.
items.explain:
Hypotenuse: 92 + 122 = 81 + 144 = 225, and √225 = 15. (225 is c2, not c; 21 is 9 + 12; 7.9 comes from subtracting: √(144 − 81) = √63 ≈ 7.9.)

Perimeter: 9 + 12 + 15 = 36 units. The choice 54 is the area (½ × 9 × 12), and 108 is 9 × 12. The choice 42 uses 21 as the hypotenuse.

items.prompt:
Each set below gives the three side lengths of a triangle.

Select two sets that form a right triangle.
items.hint: Square the two shorter sides and add. The triangle is a right triangle only if the sum equals the square of the longest side.
items.explain:
Test a2 + b2 = c2 with c as the longest side.

6, 8, 10: 36 + 64 = 100 = 102 ✓ right triangle

5, 12, 13: 25 + 144 = 169 = 132 ✓ right triangle

4, 5, 6: 16 + 25 = 41, but 62 = 36. Not right.

8, 15, 16: 64 + 225 = 289, but 162 = 256. Not right. (The right triangle with legs 8 and 15 has hypotenuse 17.)

3, 4, 6: 9 + 16 = 25, but 62 = 36. Not right. (The right triangle with legs 3 and 4 has hypotenuse 5.)

items.prompt:
The figure shows the floor plan of an L-shaped room. All corners are right angles.

What is the area of the floor?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='50,30 170,30 170,90 250,90 250,170 50,170' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='110' y='22' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>12 ft</text><text x='176' y='65' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>6 ft</text><text x='210' y='84' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>8 ft</text><text x='256' y='135' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>8 ft</text><text x='150' y='190' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>20 ft</text><text x='44' y='105' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>14 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: An L-shaped floor plan with all right angles. Going clockwise from the top-left corner: top side 12 ft, then down 6 ft, then right 8 ft, then down the right side 8 ft, bottom side 20 ft, and left side 14 ft.

items.hint: Picture the full 20 ft by 14 ft rectangle, then subtract the missing corner. Or split the L into two rectangles.
items.explain:
Method 1 (subtract): The full rectangle is 20 by 14: 20 × 14 = 280 ft2.

The missing top-right corner is 8 ft wide and 6 ft tall: 8 × 6 = 48 ft2.

280 − 48 = 232 square feet

Method 2 (add): Bottom strip: 20 × 8 = 160. Top-left part: 12 × 6 = 72. Total: 160 + 72 = 232 ft2.

The choice 280 forgets to remove the missing corner, and 328 adds the corner instead of subtracting it. The choice 68 is the perimeter: 12 + 6 + 8 + 8 + 20 + 14 = 68 feet.

items.prompt:
A window is shaped like a rectangle 4 feet wide and 6 feet tall with a half-circle on top. The diameter of the half-circle is the 4-foot top edge of the rectangle.

What is the total area of the window? Use the π key and round to the nearest tenth of a square foot.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 220' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M 110 70 A 40 40 0 0 1 190 70 Z' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='110' y='70' width='80' height='120' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='150' y='208' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>4 ft</text><text x='196' y='135' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>6 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: A window made of a rectangle 4 ft wide and 6 ft tall with a half-circle sitting on its top edge; the half-circle's diameter is the 4 ft top edge.

items.hint: Add the rectangle's area to half of a circle's area. The circle's diameter is 4 ft, so its radius is 2 ft.
items.explain:
Rectangle: 4 × 6 = 24 ft2

Half-circle: the radius is 4 ÷ 2 = 2 ft.

Full circle: π × 22 = 4π ≈ 12.566 ft2; half of it is 2π ≈ 6.283 ft2

Total: 24 + 6.283 = 30.283, which rounds to 30.3 square feet

A common mistake is using 4 as the radius: ½ × π × 16 ≈ 25.1, for a total of about 49.1. Another is adding a whole circle instead of half: 24 + 12.6 = 36.6.

items.prompt: A circular flower garden has a circumference of 62.8 feet. Using 3.14 for π, what is the area of the garden?
items.hint: Use C = 2πr to find the radius first. Then use A = πr<sup>2</sup>.
items.explain:
Find the radius from the circumference: C = 2πr

62.8 = 2 × 3.14 × r, so 62.8 = 6.28r

r = 62.8 ÷ 6.28 = 10 feet

Now the area: A = πr2 = 3.14 × 102 = 3.14 × 100 = 314 square feet

The choice 1,256 uses the diameter, 20, as the radius (3.14 × 400). The choice 31.4 multiplies π by the radius without squaring. The choice 100 is r2 without multiplying by π.
